unknowns.what_would_resolve_it: Row counts and request-rate metrics from the deployment

engine created with default pool settings (backend/app/core/db.py:5)
No metrics, tracing or load tests are committed

Login bursts can exceed the default pool size (PERF-002)

What login and password-recovery request rates are expected?

root_causes.description: Missing index on the foreign key and sort column for the item list path
Pooled DB connection held across CPU-bound hashing
Blocking external I/O on the request path
Client-controlled page size without a cap

findings.problem: Item.owner_id is a foreign key with no index, yet GET /items/ filters by it twice per request (COUNT and the page query) and orders by created_at; deleting a user also cascades through it.
findings.performance_principle: A lookup that selects a small subset of a growing table must be answered by an access path proportional to the result, not to the table.

evidence.statement: Item.owner_id is declared with foreign_key and ondelete only; no index=True.
read_items runs COUNT(*) WHERE owner_id = :id, then SELECT ... WHERE owner_id = :id ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET/LIMIT, on every list call for non-superusers.
The only create_index in migrations is ix_user_email; no migration indexes item.owner_id or item.created_at.
Superuser path has no WHERE and orders by created_at with no index on that column.
No runtime evidence (EXPLAIN, slow-query log) is committed. Planner behaviour is inferred from the absence of an index; PostgreSQL does not create indexes for FK columns automatically.

findings.conditions: Matters once the item table is large relative to a single owner's items (sequential-scan cost scales with total rows, not the owner's rows). Row counts are unknown; assumed the item table grows with user count. Negligible for a small table.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for an index on item.owner_id in models and all five migrations; none found.
Table size is unknown; a small table makes a seq scan cheap. Confidence capped at Medium for that reason.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If the item table stays in the low thousands of rows, a sequential scan is cheap and the index adds write cost for little read gain. This is a template; many deployments never reach the scale where it matters.
findings.recommendation: Add a composite index on item (owner_id, created_at) via an Alembic migration (Field(index=True) on owner_id at minimum). It serves the filter, the COUNT, the ordered page, and the FK cascade lookup on user delete.

alternatives.why: One structure serves filter and sort; avoids a sort step.
Fixes the filter but leaves a sort of the owner's rows.
Masks the scan, adds invalidation; not justified without a measured hit rate.

findings.trade_offs: Extra write cost and storage on item inserts/updates; building the index on a large table needs CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction to avoid blocking writes.

validation.metric: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) plan node type and time for the items list query for a user with few items in a large item table
validation.expectation: Seq Scan on item replaced by an index scan; time depends on the owner's item count rather than table size.
validation.falsifier: Plan already uses an index or the table is small enough that scan time is negligible.
validation.guard: Migration test; monitor p95 of GET /items/ once metrics exist.

commands.command: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM item WHERE owner_id = '<uuid>' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 100;
commands.purpose: Show the access path on a staging copy of the data.

commands.command: SELECT relname, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname IN ('item','user');
commands.purpose: Get actual row counts to resolve the table-size unknown.

findings.problem: login_access_token (sync def) looks up the user, which opens a transaction on a pooled connection, then runs an Argon2 verify (and a dummy verify for unknown emails) before the session closes. The connection and a worker thread are held across CPU-heavy hashing; no pool or concurrency configuration exists.
findings.performance_principle: Do not hold a scarce shared resource (pooled connection) across CPU-bound work that does not need it, and bound concurrency of expensive work.

evidence.statement: authenticate queries by email then calls verify_password before returning; the session from get_db stays open for the whole request.
DUMMY_HASH is an Argon2id hash encoding m=65536,t=3,p=4 (64 MiB memory parameter), so unknown-email attempts cost the same as real ones.
create_engine is called with only the URL; no pool_size, max_overflow or pool_timeout are set, so library defaults apply.
The container runs 4 workers; each has its own pool and thread pool.
get_db yields a Session for the whole request.
No rate limit or concurrency cap on /login/access-token; no runtime measurements committed.

findings.conditions: A burst of concurrent logins (or failed-login attempts) larger than the per-worker connection pool default; each in-flight verify holds a connection for its CPU time, so other endpoints can queue on the pool. Login rate and hash cost on the deployed CPU are unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Checked whether the session is released before hashing; it is not, as get_db wraps the whole request.
Argon2 verify latency is unmeasured, so impact is a risk, not a measurement.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Most deployments see low login rates, and Argon2 cost is intentional for security. If logins are rare the pool is never contended.
findings.recommendation: Release the DB connection before hashing: fetch the user, copy hashed_password, end the transaction, verify, then write the rehash only when needed. Consider a bounded concurrency limit on hashing and set pool_size/pool_timeout explicitly from worker and thread counts.

alternatives.option: Release connection before verify; bound hash concurrency
alternatives.why: Removes the shared-resource hold without weakening hashing.
Weakens security; trades away the intended property.
Raises database connection load and masks the hold.

findings.trade_offs: Slightly more code in authenticate; a concurrency cap adds queueing latency at login under bursts.

validation.metric: SQLAlchemy pool checked-out count and p95 latency of a concurrent endpoint (e.g. GET /items/) while a login burst runs
validation.expectation: Pool checkout wait during login bursts drops after the connection is released before hashing.
validation.falsifier: Pool never nears exhaustion in a burst test at the expected login rate.
validation.guard: Load-test scenario mixing login and read traffic; alert on pool wait time.

findings.problem: send_email performs a blocking SMTP exchange (emails library message.send) inline in POST /password-recovery/{email} and POST /users/. The request, its worker thread and its session wait for the mail server.
findings.performance_principle: Keep slow, failure-prone external I/O off the user-blocking path or bound it with a deadline.

evidence.statement: message.send is called synchronously; smtp_options holds host, port, tls/ssl and credentials only; no timeout key is set.
recover_password calls send_email directly after a DB lookup, so the session stays open during delivery. The endpoint is unauthenticated and sends only for existing users.
create_user also sends inline.
No background task, queue or worker exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Applies only when emails are enabled and the SMTP server is slow or unreachable; a degraded mail server then ties up worker threads and pooled connections in proportion to concurrent recovery requests. Whether the emails library applies a default socket timeout is not verified here.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for BackgroundTasks, queues or timeouts; none found.
Volume on these endpoints is expected to be low; impact depends on unmeasured mail-server health.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: These endpoints are low-volume and mail is usually fast; a template deployment may never degrade. Moving to async delivery changes error semantics.
findings.recommendation: Run delivery via FastAPI BackgroundTasks (or an external queue if durability matters) after the response, and set an explicit SMTP timeout.

alternatives.why: Smallest change that takes mail off the response path.
Heavier; only justified if delivery loss is unacceptable.

findings.trade_offs: Failures are no longer returned to the caller; background tasks are lost on process restart.

validation.metric: Latency of POST /password-recovery/{email} against an SMTP sink with injected delay
validation.expectation: Response latency independent of SMTP latency after the change.
validation.falsifier: Latency is already independent of SMTP delay, e.g. the library imposes a short timeout.
validation.guard: Test with a delayed fake SMTP server.

findings.problem: skip and limit are plain int parameters with no upper bound on /items/ and /users/. A caller can request an arbitrarily large page, materialised as ORM objects, revalidated into Pydantic models and serialised in one response. Every page also issues a separate COUNT(*).
findings.performance_principle: Bound the work and memory any single request can demand.

evidence.statement: limit: int = 100 with no le= constraint; no maximum is enforced.
Same signature on read_users.
session.exec(statement).all() then a list comprehension of ItemPublic.model_validate builds the whole page in memory.
Each call issues COUNT(*) plus the OFFSET query (two statements).

findings.conditions: A single authenticated caller with a large owned dataset (a superuser sees all items) requesting a very large limit; memory and CPU scale with the page size the client chooses. Request frequency and data volume are unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for a Query(le=...) cap or middleware limit; none in the repository (reverse proxy config not examined for body limits).

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Only authenticated users can call it and the default is 100; abuse needs a legitimate account holding many rows.
findings.recommendation: Constrain with Query(100, ge=1, le=<chosen max>) and ge=0 on skip; consider keyset pagination on (created_at, id) if deep paging is expected.

alternatives.why: One-line fix addressing the unbounded work.
Removes OFFSET cost but changes the API contract.

findings.trade_offs: Clients requesting larger pages receive a 422 and must page.

validation.metric: Peak process memory and response time for GET /items/?limit=<large> against a seeded dataset
validation.expectation: Requests above the cap are rejected before touching the database.
validation.falsifier: Large-limit requests are already rejected or memory use is flat.
validation.guard: Test asserting 422 for limit above the cap.

considered_not_reported.observation: Per-request user lookup in get_current_user (session.get by primary key)
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: One primary-key query per authenticated request; bounded and indexed, no evidence of cost beyond baseline.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Profiling shows the user lookup dominating authenticated request latency.

considered_not_reported.observation: ORM cascade delete of items on user self-delete
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Rare operation bounded by one user's item count; ondelete CASCADE also exists in the database.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Users with very large item counts are deleted frequently.

adjacent_findings.problem: The unauthenticated /login/access-token endpoint has no rate limit or lockout, so repeated password attempts are limited only by hashing cost.

evidence.statement: No rate-limiting dependency or middleware in app/main.py or the routes; the login handler is open.

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Add rate limiting at the proxy or application layer.
adjacent_findings.assessed_properly_by: A dedicated security review of authentication and abuse controls
